stories.headline: 96 vs 86: Abhishek leaves Sooryavanshi chasing as six-hitting race takes a twist
stories.deck: Abhishek Sharma added 11 more sixes to his tally on Thursday, smashing 108 off just 34 balls against Afghanistan in the third and final T20I at the Arun Jaitley Stadium in Delhi. His breathtaking knock included a 30-ball century, the fastest T20I hundred by an Indian batter. It was also the fastest century by a batter from a Full Member nation against another Full Member nation.
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The six-hitting battle between Abhishek Sharma and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has taken an interesting turn in 2026. Abhishek has now moved 10 sixes ahead of Sooryavanshi, with the India opener hitting 96 sixes in all T20 cricket this year compared to the youngster's 86.
Abhishek added 11 more sixes to his tally on Thursday, smashing 108 off just 34 balls against Afghanistan in the third and final T20I at the Arun Jaitley Stadium in Delhi.
His breathtaking knock included a 30-ball century, the fastest T20I hundred by an Indian batter. It was also the fastest century by a batter from a Full Member nation against another Full Member nation.
Abhishek leads Sooryavanshi in six-hitting
Abhishek's 96 sixes in 2026 are the second-most by an Indian batter in a calendar year in all T20s.
His own record stands at 108 sixes, which he hit in 2025. He also hit 87 sixes in 2024.
Sooryavanshi's 86 sixes in 2026 are currently fourth on the list.
India batters with most sixes in a calendar year in all T20s
While Abhishek has hit more sixes overall in 2026, Sooryavanshi has cleared the boundary more frequently, hitting one six every 4.99 balls compared to Abhishek's 6.64.
Abhishek's 11 sixes against Afghanistan
Abhishek produced another power-hitting masterclass against Afghanistan.
He smashed 108 off just 34 balls, hitting 11 sixes and nine fours. 
It was his third century in T20Is.
Most of his sixes went straight over the bowler's head. He attacked both pace and spin and kept finding the boundary throughout his innings.
With India batting first for the first time in the series, Abhishek made full use of the opportunity.
He brought up his fifty off just 16 balls before completing his century off 30 balls.
Fastest T20I century by a Full Member batter
Abhishek's 30-ball century was the fastest T20I hundred by a batter from a Full Member nation.
He went past the previous mark of 33 balls, jointly held by Zimbabwe's Sikandar Raza and New Zealand's Finn Allen.
It was also the fastest century by a batter from a Full Member nation against another Full Member nation.
Fastest T20I hundreds by batters from Full Member teams
Abhishek also broke former India captain Rohit Sharma's record for the fastest T20I century by an Indian. Rohit had scored his century off 35 balls against Sri Lanka in Indore in 2017.
Abhishek among India's biggest six-hitters
Abhishek's 11 sixes against Afghanistan also put him second on the list of most sixes by an Indian batter in a T20I innings.
He is behind only his own record of 13 sixes, which he hit against England in Mumbai in 2025.
Most sixes by an Indian batter in a T20I innings
India race to 100 in powerplay
Abhishek's six-hitting helped India race to 100 for no loss in the first six overs.
It was India's highest score in the powerplay in T20Is.
Sanju Samson also played his part, scoring a fluent 50 off 35 balls for his second successive fifty-plus score.
With both India openers in good form, Sooryavanshi has not got an opportunity in the playing XI in the series.
Abhishek's special celebration
Abhishek completed his century in the ninth over.
He reached 99 with a powerful pull off Abdullah Ahmadzai before taking a single to bring up his hundred.
He then removed his helmet, sat on the ground and celebrated with a meditation pose as the Delhi crowd applauded the special innings.
India eventually finished on 221 for seven. Afghanistan restricted India to 37 runs in the final five overs and picked up four wickets during that period.

stories.headline: Asian Games 2026 | Willstrop punts on Anahat becoming unplayable as she matures physically and tactically
stories.deck: The Englishman, who’s part of the coaching staff for the Asian Games-bound Indian squash contingent, believes Anahat Singh’s instinctive attacking game makes her a “very unusual player
stories.bodyText:
Former World No. 1 James Willstrop, who’s part of the coaching staff for the Asian Games-bound Indian squash contingent, believes Anahat Singh’s instinctive attacking game makes her a “very unusual player.”
“She’s got this instinct to go into the front of the court and to hit accurately short. I’ve very rarely seen it being done the way she’s doing it by someone as good as she is,” ,” he said at the Indian Squash Academy (ISA) on Thursday, ahead of the squash contingent’s departure for Japan on Friday.
“I mean, she’s a very unusual player. Unusual in that she attacks the front so clinically and more often than the other girls. So, the other girls are constantly on edge.”
Anahat, the reigning World junior champion, is still “very young” and “relatively inexperienced compared to her compatriots,” Willstrop said.
“She’s a baby. She’s barely played any platinum events. She’s up against them, but then she’s probably got a little bit less pressure than they have,” he added.
Willstrop expects the 18-year-old to become increasingly difficult to beat as she develops physically and tactically.
“The girls are already struggling with her now because of her sheer instinct and attack. Give her a few more years. When she gets the physical strength, becomes even more disciplined, and gets even more understanding of constructing rallies, it’s going to be a real nightmare for the opponents. She’s a wonderful prospect,” he said.
The 43-year-old sees his role at the Asian Games as primarily providing “tactical support,” while helping the players make the most of his “experience.”
Speaking about India’s singles medal prospects, he said: “Anahat’s obviously a big prospect for a medal chance — that could be gold. Abhay (Singh) and Veer (Chotrani) have great chances.
“I’ve seen Veer push Ali Farag very hard at the World Championships. I’ve seen him play some fabulous squash. If he can produce that, there’s a massive chance of a medal.”

stories.headline: Abhishek blazes fastest century in full-member T20s
stories.deck: The 26-year-old hammered ​108 off 34 balls, striking nine fours and ⁠11 sixes before falling to Rashid Khan. His hundred eclipsed the previous India record of a 35-ball century set by stalwart Rohit Sharma against Sri Lanka ‌in 2017
stories.bodyText:
India opener Abhishek Sharma smashed the fastest Twenty20 International century by a batter from a full-member nation on Thursday (September 17, 2026), blasting a 30-ball hundred as the hosts thrashed Afghanistan by 127 runs in Delhi to complete a 3-0 series sweep.
The 26-year-old hammered 108 off 34 balls, striking nine fours and 11 sixes before falling to Rashid Khan. His hundred eclipsed the previous India record of a 35-ball century set by stalwart Rohit Sharma against Sri Lanka in 2017.
Fellow opener and wicketkeeper-batter Sanju Samson chipped in with 50 off 35 deliveries as India posted 221-7 after Afghanistan won the toss and chose to bowl.
Afghanistan's reply never took off as the visitors slumped to 47-4 and were eventually bowled out for 94 in 14.1 overs. Captain Ibrahim Zadran was the only Afghanistan batter to cross 20, making 25, while India all-rounder Nitish Kumar Reddy and spinner Ravi Bishnoi dismantled the batting lineup with three wickets apiece.
‘Very important for captain, coach to be on your side’
"I feel it's all dependent on my process before every series," Abhishek said. "It's very particular for me, against who I play and their bowlers, how I'm going to utilise the powerplay... The way I play, it's very important for the captain and the coach to be on your side.
"You have to get surety. I feel this is because of them as well... It's very simple from day one. I just want to express myself. Just see the ball and hit the ball.
"You can't be sure you'll be doing well all the time, but the culture we've developed in our team is to dominate, and it's been going well so far."
India had already wrapped up the series with a seven-wicket victory in the second T20 on Tuesday (September 15, 2026), having opened the contest with another convincing seven-wicket win on Sunday.
"Definitely disappointed," Zadran said. "We improved a little bit in the powerplay. Totally happy with the intent...
"Yes, we will struggle a little bit in one or two series, but with time we will improve. If we don't have intent, it is really hard to beat international teams.
"We need to play more games and more series, especially against the biggest teams. That's how we can improve."
India next face Japan in a one-off T20 on September 22 before beginning their Asian Games campaign at the quarter-final stage six days later.

briefs.headline: Abhishek Sharma opens up on Gill-Gambhir backing after record 30-ball century
briefs.deck: Abhishek Sharma made the most of that freedom on Thursday, smashing a record 30-ball century against Afghanistan in the third and final T20I in Delhi. His 108 off 34 balls, which included 11 sixes, helped India post 221/7 and complete a 3-0 series sweep with a 127-run win.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Abhishek Sharma
 believes the backing of captain Shreyas Iyer and head coach 
Gautam Gambhir
 has played an important role in allowing him to play his natural game.
Abhishek made the most of that freedom on Thursday, smashing a record 30-ball century against Afghanistan in the third and final T20I in Delhi. His 108 off 34 balls, which included 11 sixes, helped India post 221/7 and complete a 3-0 series sweep with a 127-run win.
The left-hander was named both Player of the Match and Player of the Series after finishing the three-match series with 209 runs.
Speaking after his match-winning knock, Abhishek said the team culture and the support of the captain and coach have allowed him to express himself without worrying about failures.
"I've told in the first interview as well. We've been doing this last two years. One or two bad series won't define us as a batting department. We wanted to dominate throughout the whole year before the world cup no matter who the opposition is. I feel as a batter, sometimes you have up and downs. The most important thing is as a team we have to be together and support each other. That's how these innings happen," Abhishek said at thye post match presentation.
"I feel it's all dependent on my process before every series. It's very particular for me, against who I play and their bowlers. How I'm going to utilise the powerplay. Who's going to bowl the powerplay, the 7th over, the 8th over," he said.
"And the way I play, it's very important for the captain and the coach to be on your side. You have to get surety. I feel this is because of them as well. I feel I don't want to restrict any area. It's just watch the ball and play according to it. It's very simple from day one. I just want to express myself. Just see the ball and hit the ball. You can't be sure you'll be doing well all the time but the culture we've developed in our team is to dominate and it's been going well so far," Abhishek said.
Abhishek turns dead rubber into his night
With India having already sealed the series, the third T20I was a dead rubber. Abhishek, however, ensured there was little doubt about where the spotlight would be. It was the first time in the series that India batted first and Abhishek immediately went after the Afghanistan attack. He brought up his fifty from just 16 balls and then completed his hundred in the ninth over.
He reached 99 with a powerful pull off Abdullah Ahmadzai before taking a single to reach three figures. He then removed his helmet and celebrated with a seated meditation pose as the crowd rose to applaud him. His 108 came from only 34 balls and included 11 sixes and nine fours. It was the fastest T20I century by an Indian batter, beating Rohit Sharma's 35-ball hundred against Sri Lanka in 2017.
It was also the fastest T20I hundred by a batter from a Test-playing nation against another Test-playing nation, surpassing Finn Allen's 33-ball century against South Africa earlier this year.
India race to 100 in six overs
Abhishek's attack gave India a flying start. India reached 100 without losing a wicket in the powerplay, their highest score in the first six overs of a T20 match.
Afghanistan struggled to contain him from the beginning. Azmat Omarzai conceded 17 runs in the second over, while Fazalhaq Farooqi gave away 23 in the third.
Captain Ibrahim Zadran turned to spin during the powerplay, but that did little to stop Abhishek. Sanju Samson also joined the attack, hitting two straight sixes off Mohammad Nabi before Abhishek cleared the boundary twice in the same over, which cost Afghanistan 29 runs.
Samson, dropped on 22 at mid-off by Zadran, went on to score 50 off 35 balls for his second successive fifty-plus score.
Abhishek's departure in the 10th over came with India on 142/1. India eventually finished on 221/7 after losing four wickets and scoring 37 runs in the final five overs.
Afghanistan collapse again
Afghanistan's batting once again failed to put India under pressure. They were bowled out for 94 in 14.1 overs, giving India a 127-run win.
Nitish Kumar Reddy opened the bowling for India and conceded 15 runs in his first over before returning later to claim three wickets. Axar Patel removed Rahmanullah Gurbaz and Sediqullah Atal during the powerplay, while Jasprit Bumrah produced a sharp yorker to dismiss Darwish Rasooli. Yash Thakur then accounted for Ibrahim Zadran in the sixth over.
Afghanistan were 47/4 at that stage and never recovered.
Both teams will now head to the 
Asian Games
.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026 | Bangladesh advance without playing; Pakistan scrape past Thailand to reach semifinals
briefs.deck: Bangladesh will take on the winner of the quarterfinal between India and Japan, due to be played on Friday (September 18, 2026), in the semifinals scheduled for September 20
briefs.bodyText:
Bangladesh entered the semifinals without even stepping on to the field, while Pakistan had to toil hard against unfancied Thailand in a low-scoring thriller before booking their last-four spot in the Asian Games women's cricket competition here on Thursday (September 17, 2026).
Bangladesh advanced on the basis of their higher international ranking after their quarterfinal match against China was abandoned due to a wet outfield. The T20 match was called off without even the toss taking place at the Karogi Sports Park in Aichi prefecture's Nisshin city.
Bangladesh are currently ranked 10th in the ICC's T20 International standings, while China is way down at the 36th position.
Pakistan, on the other hand, won by three wickets after being a set a target of 92 by Thailand in a truncated match due to wet conditions.
Bangladesh will take on the winner of the quarterfinal between India and Japan, due to be played on Friday (September 18, 2026), in the semifinals scheduled for September 20. Pakistan will square off against the winner of the Sri Lanka-Malaysia clash, also on Friday.
The Harmanpreet Kaur-led India are the defending champions in the competition that features only eight teams and began from the quarterfinal stage.
The Pakistan-Thailand clash also got off to a delayed start at the same venue due to the ground conditions and was eventually truncated to 11-overs-a-side.
Opting to bowl after winning the toss, the unheralded Thai batters gave a good account of themselves by posting 91/4 with wicket-keeper and number three Nannapat Koncharoenkai top-scoring with a 38-ball 49 that featured seven fours.
In reply, it was a typically erratic performance by Pakistan with wickets falling regularly.
Shawaal Zulfiqar (25) and Fatima Sana (21) were the only notable contributors as their batting collapsed despite a relatively gettable target on the board.
For Thailand, off-spinners Onnicha Kamchomphu (3/37) and Sunida Chaturongrattana (2/23) did well for the side.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026 | Japan embracing the occasion of facing India in cricket rather than fearing it
briefs.deck: India Women begin their Asian Games campaign against the host on September 18 at Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin
briefs.bodyText:
Alan Curr remembers V.V.S. Laxman’s 281.
He was at university when Laxman played one of Test cricket’s greatest innings against Australia at the Eden Gardens in Kolkata in 2001. Twenty-five years later, Curr, now Chief Operating Officer of the Japan Cricket Association (JCA), found himself on the phone with Laxman, only this time the Indian legend was asking the questions.
Laxman, now coach of the Indian men’s team travelling to the Games, wanted to know what to expect in Japan.
“Certainly in the two or three minutes leading up to the call, you’re like, wow, I saw this guy play a lot of cricket,” Curr tells Sportstar.
The call lasted only a few minutes, but it neatly captured Japan’s changing place in the cricket world. India was no longer simply a team Curr watched from afar. It was now a team Japan had to prepare to host.
India Women begin their Asian Games campaign against the host on September 18 at Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin.
India’s players are full-time professionals with contracts and endorsements; Japan’s women remain amateur and failed to qualify for the 2022 Asian Games tournament. Yet Japan is embracing the occasion rather than fearing it.
“It is incredibly exciting, I have waited a decade to play in the Asian Games, so finally being able to compete on home soil is something special,” says captain Mai Yanagida.
The fixture has reshaped expectations for the JCA. India’s visit has driven ticket demand the federation has never recorded, forcing it to plan for security, crowds and media.
“For years, our biggest problem was finding players to come and play matches... Whereas when you’ve got India coming, then the tickets sold out in about — it felt like about 20 minutes,” Curr says.
The stakes go beyond one result. When Japan’s men made their Asian Games debut in Hangzhou three years ago and beat Cambodia, it became national news, with highlights on major television channels — cricket briefly gaining an Olympics-style ripple.
For the women, though, cricket is still a second career squeezed around work and study. Japan has only 14 clubs, and players juggle the sport with jobs, teaching or university.
“We are not full-time professional cricketers... It definitely requires a lot of personal sacrifices,” Yanagida says.
Kurumi Ota, a systems engineer at Hitachi, knows that cost. She stepped away from the sport for seven years because of work before returning.
“When I first started playing cricket, we would sometimes practise under overpasses... Today there are international-standard grounds and grass outfields,” she says.
The JCA now has a 20-year vision to grow not just players but coaches, commentators and curators.
On September 18, Japan gets its biggest cricketing stage yet.
“I mean how often do you get to say you had V.V.S Laxman talk to you about cricket,” Curr says.

briefs.headline: Cold blood, hot streak: Elena Rybakina’s US Open triumph and her quiet rise to World No. 1
briefs.deck: An Achilles injury, just four days of practice, and a final against the top seed and two-time defending champion... Rybakina’s path to the US Open title was anything but simple. However, her tennis made it look that way. In the process, she ascended to the top of the world rankings.
briefs.bodyText:
Sport has an old rule about momentum: catch fire late in a season, and the off-season usually douses it. That sentiment holds for most part. But, as with most things in life, there are exceptions. Elena Rybakina’s is one.
The Russian-born Kazakh couldn’t get past the fourth round at the Grand Slams last year. Form looked to have deserted her and the season was all set to be chalked up as yet another ‘learning experience’ in her career.
Then, it all changed.
She came through a tough set of tournaments in September and October, won in Ningbo and closed the year by defeating Aryna Sabalenka in the WTA Finals title decider, taking home more than $five million in prize money, the largest purse in women’s tennis history at that time.
The soft-spoken 27-year-old later disappeared for the off-season. When she resumed action, she picked up from where she had left off, looking just as dangerous as she’d been. Rybakina reached the Australian Open final without dropping a set, clawed back from 0-3 down in the third set to beat Sabalenka again for her second Major. She became the first player in eight years to win the WTA Finals and the Australian Open in succession.
What followed was, by any measure, a strong season: a title in Stuttgart along with runner-up finishes at Indian Wells and the Canadian Open. She also banked her 400th career win on the way.
The underlying numbers are absurd. Since last year’s US Open, nobody on the Tour has won more matches than Rybakina (62) and nobody has beaten more top-10 players (16, with a 16-6 record). She leads the field in winners (1,569), in aces (394) and break points saved (65.5%). She made six finals (tied with Jessica Pegula for most on the Tour) and clinched four crowns, more than anyone else.
READ | Stability at the top: On the tennis and the U.S. Open
Put it all together and you get a first-time World No. 1: the first from Kazakhstan, and at 27 years and 89 days, the second-oldest woman ever to reach the summit for the first time. She rose to the top, tournament by tournament, so relentlessly that by the time it actually happened, nobody blinked.
And yet a year ago, the idea of Rybakina dethroning Sabalenka looked unthinkable, unattainable even. Last September, she had 3,833 points to Sabalenka’s 11,225 — barely a third. By last month, that gap had shrunk to 360 points, before she finally ended Sabalenka’s 99-week reign as the No. 1.
Even before she ascended to the top of the rankings, Rybakina had already beaten a reigning World No. 1 nine times, a mark bettered only by Gabriela Sabatini’s 10. The Kazakh has now beaten nine of the last 10 women who have held the top ranking. Only Ashleigh Barty got away.
Crowning moment
Impressive as all that is, the true crowning moment of Rybakina’s year came at Flushing Meadows; she barely stumbled, let alone look anywhere near beatable. The strange part is that heading into the tournament, nobody was asking how far she’d go. They were instead wondering if she’d play at all.
On August 14, she was steam-rollered by Iga Swiatek to the Canadian Open title. A week later, Rybakina was forced to retire after just five games of her Cincinnati quarterfinal against the same opponent.
An Achilles injury was suspected, though little else was confirmed. In the week before the US Open, Rybakina barely picked up a racquet. As far as preparation for one of the biggest titles in the sport goes, it was far from ideal.
“It wasn’t the best time, for sure, because I was so upset. I didn’t know how it was going to be, day by day. We arrived in New York, did an MRI and it didn’t look that great. We had to talk with a lot of doctors to get an opinion on what we should do,” she said, hours after conquering New York.
She started practising just four days before the US Open got underway and with each match, she looked less like a woman shaking off rust and more like one reminding everyone who she was. The power was there and the aces were pulled out of nowhere when they were needed the most.
“Just four days of practice, a lot of belief in myself and talking with the team non-stop about the tactics... that’s how I played in Canada, how I played in Cincinnati. I mean, it’s just so many things. Everything went my way. I’m shocked.”
Her tennis over the fortnight told a different story. Nothing about this triumph was shocking. Everything came together for Rybakina one way or the other.
Sabalenka loves to feast on her opponent’s second serves, as Pegula was harshly reminded in the semifinals. So when Rybakina landed just eight of her 30 first serves in the opening set of the final, logic dictated that the Belarusian would seize control of the contest.
The logic was wrong. Rybakina pulled out heavier, quicker second serves and deep, powerful groundstrokes to put Sabalenka on the back foot. If one moment captured how the final unfolded, it was the last game of the opening set, where Rybakina couldn’t hit a first serve but ended up on top despite everything thrown at her.
By the end of the night, as she did at the WTA Finals, Rybakina had a trophy and a fat cheque in hand, but this time as World No. 1. Four years ago, she barely managed a smile after conquering Wimbledon, and the tennis world wondered if she’d ever let herself feel a title the way champions are supposed to. In New York, something shifted. The fists were raised, the celebration stayed brief; however, underneath it, for the first time, was an unmistakable and hard-earned joy.
Rybakina wins the way glaciers move: silently, relentlessly, until you look up one day and the entire landscape has changed. New York didn’t just hand her a trophy; it handed women’s tennis a warning wrapped in ice — quiet on the outside, catastrophic on the inside.
A year earlier, after finishing runner-up to Rybakina at the WTA Finals, Sabalenka — far from being tennis’ most gracious loser — was overheard reaching for a Russian idiom that translated to: “Once a year, even a stick shoots,” suggesting Rybakina’s form was little more than a fluke. Famous last words.
Overcoming controversy
Like most of the sport’s best players, Rybakina hasn’t always made headlines for the right reasons. First came the injuries and health scares that dragged her out of tournaments through 2024 and ’25. Then her ‘worrying’ relationship with coach Stefano Vukov landed under the microscope.
In September 2024, she fired Vukov and hired Novak Djokovic’s former coach Goran Ivanisevic, before reinstating Vukov. A WTA investigation later found that Vukov had engaged in abusive conduct towards Rybakina, and he was banned from coaching at WTA events in January 2025. The ban was overturned on appeal that August.
Rybakina never softened her stance towards the WTA through it all, even declining to pose for a photo with the then-CEO Portia Archer after beating Sabalenka to win the WTA Finals on November 8.
Long before the WTA formally looked into the Vukov relationship, fans and pundits had already suspected that something was off. He was always very vocal in relentlessly criticising during matches, well beyond any reasonable idea of ‘tough love’ coaching.
One can argue that Vukov has been noticeably softer since the ban ended. Criticism has largely given way to encouragement. Optimists will call it a man who learnt his lesson. Cynics will call it a man who learnt to behave when the cameras were rolling.
ALSO READ | Federer’s final masterpiece: Roger’s homecoming to the Hall of Fame
Rybakina herself has stayed quiet on the specifics, but she’s hinted that having her team back in place has mattered.
“I think I have a very good team and good people around me now. It definitely helps. A lot was going on in the previous year outside of the court. I think now all my focus is on tennis. I can’t always perform at my best. There are always ups and downs, but I think we’ve been doing a very good job, taking the right decisions in certain situations, because every day is a challenge,” she said last week.
The Vukov chapter may never be fully closed in public, but it changes nothing about where Rybakina stands right now. What once looked like a hot streak has long since stopped resembling one. Nothing about her has come out as a fluke.
She will now head into tournaments, starting with the China Open later this month, as the top seed and a clear title favourite. Given how balanced she is in success and adversity, none of that seems likely to rattle her.
“I feel like you will appreciate and think about it [becoming World No. 1] even more when you finish your career. For now, you need to keep going. You never know how long you’re going to stay. All my thoughts are just for the next match,” she said after her quarterfinal win over Qinwen Zheng.
Call it humility. Call it how elite athletes are wired. Call it a deliberate way of shrugging off the spotlight before it gets too heavy. Whatever it is, one thing isn’t up for debate: the girl who once played tennis as an after-school pastime, who didn’t consider it a career until she was 17, has walked out of New York as the most dominant force in women’s tennis. Rybakina is pure potential energy, coiled at the very peak of her arc. Buckle up.

briefs.headline: Afghanistan vs India third T20I: Abhishek’s hurricane hundred powers Men in Blue’s emphatic series sweep
briefs.deck: The left-hander’s record-breaking 34-ball 108 and fellow-opener Samson’s fifty take India to 221 for seven; the Afghans get bundled out for 94
briefs.bodyText:
Six-hitting is a skill that Abhishek Sharma has honed to perfection. He can make it appear ridiculously easy, as though he is playing around with a joystick in a video game, but make no mistake: few can do what the 26-year-old does time and again in the T20 version. A sublime example came in the third T20I against Afghanistan at the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Thursday as Abhishek hammered a record-breaking 34-ball 108, studded with nine fours and 11 sixes, to take India to 221 for seven.
With Afghanistan capitulating for 94 in response, Shreyas Iyer & Co. completed a resounding 127-run win for a 3-0 sweep. Nitish Kumar struck thrice in an over while Ravi Bishnoi also provided three breakthroughs.
Abhishek’s century took merely 30 balls, the fastest against a Test-playing nation and the third-quickest in all in this format. Sanju Samson chipped in with 50 off 35 balls, forging a sensational opening stand of 142 in 9.5 overs. The surface appeared to be a shirtfront when Abhishek and Samson were on song, but the others didn’t find it as easy.
Abhishek imposed himself straightaway. In the second over, Azmatullah Omarzai felt the pinch. The first of the opener’s maximums came when he swivelled and pulled effortlessly beyond deep square-leg. Omarzai persisted with the shorter length and paid the price. Off the fourth ball, he pulled out a forehand slap past mid-on for four. Two deliveries later, he made room and slashed a back-of-a-length delivery over cover for another six.
Having quickly sized up the Afghan attack, the southpaw’s carnage found a higher gear. The next over, bowled by Fazalhaq Farooqi, went for 23 runs as the Punjab lad stitched together a sequence that read 6, 6, 4, 4.
Afghanistan turned to spin early in the hope of disturbing India’s rhythm. Instead, Samson, who had scored three off his first seven balls, joined the six-hitting party. In the fourth over, he deposited Mujeeb Ur Rahman over long-on.
What followed was a 29-run over by experienced off-spinner Mohammad Nabi as the openers took turns to flex their firepower. By the time ace leggie Rashid Khan conceded 15 runs in the final over of the PowerPlay, India had raced to 100 for none.
In the ninth over, Abhishek entered the record books by reaching the three-figure mark. Ironically, his celebration was unlike the action that had transpired till then: he took off his helmet, sat down and soaked in the moment with a meditative pose.

briefs.headline: Abhishek Sharma's record 30-ball century powers India to 3-0 T20I series sweep
briefs.deck: Abhishek Sharma's returns in international cricket haven't been the best since the T20I World Cup in March. The runs have come at a premium for him. He wasn't going to let this opportunity re-establish himself as India's undisputed first-choice opener in T20Is even as the buzz around 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi only keeps growing. He finished the series with 209 runs off 85 balls.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: If you were seated on the second tier here at the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Thursday evening, the white Kookaburra ball would have seemed to be perpetually flying in your eyeline for the first 10 overs of the third T20I between India and Afghanistan. It was 
Abhishek Sharma
 who was bringing a dead rubber to life just the way Indian T20 batters are used to doing in home conditions and the IPL.
Such are the standards set by Abhishek over the last three years that bringing up his hundred off 30 balls felt like just another day in the office. As one was still coming to terms with the carnage he inflicted, Abhishek decided to celebrate his century by calmly sitting in the middle of the pitch, meditating like a monk.
Having endured a comparatively modest year with the bat in international cricket, Abhishek's relentless hitting was kind of a throwback to his marauding run with the Indian team before the T20 World Cup in March.
Abhishek's onslaught on a tired pitch made his opening partner 
Sanju Samson
's 35-ball 50 look like a laborious effort. That one knock of 108 off 34 balls, which ended in the 10th over, was enough for India to post 221/7 after Abhishek left the park with the scoreboard reading 142/1.
The 11 sixes and nine boundaries off Abhishek's bat were enough to break the spirits of the Afghanistan team. Afghanistan's batting folded for 94 in just [missing number] overs to lose by 127 runs, bringing their first 'home' series against India to an end with a 3-0 scoreline in favour of India.
The Afghan players clearly lacked energy on the field, having endured heavy poundings in the first two T20Is here this week. It appeared they almost waited for this game to just pass by. But Abhishek wasn't satiated despite his two whirlwind knocks in the previous two matches.
As the Afghan players looked like merely rolling their arms over and tossing the ball without any intent, Abhishek was amusing himself by testing the catching skills of the spectators in the stands.
Abhishek's returns in international cricket haven't been the best since the T20I World Cup in March. The runs have come at a premium for him. He wasn't going to let this opportunity go to waste in re-establishing himself as India's undisputed first-choice opener in T20Is even as the buzz around 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi only keeps growing. He finished the series with 209 runs off 85 balls.
Reddy's bowling gives confidence
Nitish Kumar Reddy is the pet project for the team management to get him ready as a premier seam-bowling allrounder besides the injury-prone Hardik Pandya. On Thursday, he managed just one off four balls with the bat in his only outing in the series.
Captain Shreyas Iyer chose to give him the new ball like Pandya has been doing in T20 cricket for India. The first one didn't look incisive, but Reddy came back later in the innings with a clear plan of varying the pace and length. He finished with figures of 3/25 in four overs.
Having pulled him out of the Asian Games team, Reddy's performance on Thursday night will give the team management a lot of confidence as they start preparing for the ODI World Cup with the ODI series against West Indies later this month.

briefs.headline: Chess Olympiad: Nihal saves the day for India; women have it easy
briefs.bodyText:
Nihal Sarin saved the blushes for India on day two of the Chess Olympiad at Samarkand. His win on the second board was the reason why India, the defending champion, could beat a much lower-rated Indonesia 2.5-1.5 in the Open section on Thursday.
Nihal, though, was in considerable trouble in his game against Arif Abdul Hafiz before he won in 37 moves. R. Praggnanandhaa, the in-form player who was making his first appearance in this edition of the Olympiad, World champion D. Gukesh and Vidit Gujrathi were all forced to draw their games.
Praggnanandhaa did try his best to stretch his opponent Susanto Megaranto, who, however, played solidly to ensure that the drawn rook-pawn endgame was indeed drawn, after 79 moves.
The Indian women, also the reigning champions, were more convincing than the men, just as they were in the opening round. They beat Finland 3.5-0.5.
There were wins for Divya Deshmukh, Vantika Agrawal and B. Savitha Shri, but on the top board, R. Vaishali, like her brother Praggnanandhaa, had to settle for a draw, with Anastasia Keinanen in 88 moves. So the top-seeded Indian women could not quite score the full points, which they had in the opening round against Dominican Republic (4-0).
